title: A Stone No One Had Seen on the Seabed Was Still a Family's Fortune
hook: A storm sank a stone, yet the islanders said it kept its owner

open.title: A family called rich because of a stone no one had ever seen
open.line: Yap, a small island in Micronesia. One family here was called rich over a stone not even they had ever seen.

summary: On Yap, stone money usually stayed put. Even a stone a storm sank was agreed not lost.

text: Yap islanders say a huge stone wheel lies on the seabed.
And it's said that stone still has an owner.
On Yap, stone wheels with a hole in the middle were money.
The big ones are 3.6 m across.
It was quarried on Palau, hundreds of kilometers away.

panels.text: How do you even pay with a stone that big?

text: Big stones usually stay put. Only the owner changes.
Once the village knows the new owner, it's done.
Long ago, a family's ancestor was rafting a big stone home when a storm hit.
To survive, they cut the raft loose, and the stone sank.
Actually, the seabed made no difference.
It wasn't the owner's fault, so everyone agreed it wasn't lost.
In 1903, a visiting American scholar heard about that family.
For generations not even the family saw it, yet no one doubted their wealth.
In 2010, an anthropologist said of Yap's oral history:
Even a stone no one has seen in over 100 years has an owner today.

sources: Milton Friedman, The Island of Stone Money (Hoover Institution, 1991)
NPR Planet Money: The Island Of Stone Money (2010)
